essentials: The ESRS are the **mandatory standards** for CSRD reporting. They define what a sustainability statement contains, down to the individual datapoint.
Set 1 has **12 standards**: two cross-cutting ones and ten on environmental, social and governance topics.
Only **ESRS 2** (general disclosures) applies to everyone. All topical content depends on the company's **materiality assessment**.
Set 1 is in use for reports up to financial year 2026 and is **replaced by the revised ESRS from financial year 2027**.

sections.title: What the standards are for
text: The CSRD only says that companies must report on sustainability matters. Without detailed standards, every company would again choose its own content, as under the NFRD. The ESRS fix the topics, the structure, the definitions and the metrics, so that reports can be compared and audited.

They were drafted by **EFRAG** and adopted by the Commission as a delegated act in July 2023 (Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2772). As a regulation, the standards apply directly: there are no national versions.

sections.title: How the materiality assessment works
text: The assessment decides which topical standards and datapoints a company reports. It looks at **impacts, risks and opportunities**, usually shortened to IROs.
steps: **Understand the context**: activities, business relationships, locations, affected stakeholders, across the company's own operations and its value chain.
**Identify** actual and potential impacts on people and the environment, and the risks and opportunities that sustainability matters create for the company.
**Assess impact materiality** by severity (scale, scope and how hard the harm is to remedy) and, for potential impacts, likelihood.
**Assess financial materiality** by the size and likelihood of financial effects over the short, medium and long term.
**Decide and document** which topics are material, and report the process itself under ESRS 2.
after: If a company concludes that climate change is not material, Set 1 requires a detailed explanation. For other topics a brief explanation may be given.

sections.title: How a disclosure is built
text: Every topical standard follows the same four areas, mirroring the structure used by the international climate disclosure frameworks:
points: **Strategy**: how the topic interacts with the business model.
**Impact, risk and opportunity management**: the policies and actions in place.
**Metrics and targets**: measurable results and goals.
after: A useful shorthand is **policies, actions, targets, metrics**. If a company has no policy or target for a material topic, it says so; the ESRS require transparency, not a particular level of performance.

sections.title: Reliefs for the first years
text: Set 1 phases in the hardest datapoints, such as anticipated financial effects and parts of the value-chain information. A ‘quick fix’ delegated act of July 2025 extended these reliefs for wave 1 companies, so that they do not have to add new datapoints for financial years 2025 and 2026 just before the standards are replaced.
For financial year 2026, companies may keep using Set 1 or move early to the revised ESRS. From financial year 2027 only the revised standards apply.

terms.text: Impacts, risks and opportunities: the three things the materiality assessment identifies for each sustainability matter.
The company's actual or potential effects on people and the environment, judged by severity and likelihood. The inside-out view.
Sustainability matters that trigger financial effects on the company. The outside-in view.
A single item of information required by a standard, narrative or numeric. Set 1 has more than 1,000.
A group of datapoints on one subject, such as E1-6 on gross greenhouse gas emissions.
ESRS 1 and ESRS 2, which apply regardless of topic.
Information on a material matter that no standard covers, which the company must still report.
The body that drafts the standards as technical adviser to the Commission.

mistakes.right: Apart from ESRS 2, a company reports only on topics its assessment found material, and within them only material information.

mistakes.wrong: The ESRS oblige companies to have a climate target or a human-rights policy.
mistakes.right: They are disclosure standards. A company without a policy or target reports that fact. Obligations to act come from other laws.

mistakes.wrong: The ESRS and the CSRD are the same thing.
mistakes.right: The CSRD is the directive that creates the duty to report. The ESRS are the delegated act with the content of the report.

mistakes.wrong: Financial materiality is what matters most; impact materiality is optional.
mistakes.right: Both count equally. Impact materiality alone makes a topic reportable.

practice: Start every reporting cycle with the **list of material IROs** and map each to the disclosure requirements that follow from it.
Treat **ESRS 2** as the backbone: it explains governance, strategy and the materiality process and links to the topical sections.
For each material topic, write down **policy, action, target, metric**, and state openly where one is missing.
Keep an **evidence file** for every material judgement. The assurance provider will ask how you reached it.
Plan the **move to the revised ESRS**: for financial year 2026 compare the effort of staying on Set 1 with switching early.

quiz.q: Which ESRS standard must every reporting company apply, whatever its materiality assessment says?
quiz.why: ESRS 2 is mandatory for all. The topical standards apply only where the topic is material.

quiz.q: How many standards does ESRS Set 1 contain?
quiz.why: Two cross-cutting standards (ESRS 1 and 2), five environmental, four social and one governance standard.

quiz.q: Which three factors determine the severity of an impact?
options: Size of company, sector and region
quiz.why: Severity is judged by how grave the impact is (scale), how widespread (scope) and how hard it is to put right (irremediable character).

quiz.q: A company has no biodiversity policy, although biodiversity is a material topic. What do the ESRS require?
options: It must adopt a policy before publishing the report
It must disclose that it has no policy
It may leave the topic out of the report
It must commission an external biodiversity audit
quiz.why: The ESRS require transparency. Where no policy, action or target exists, the company states that.

quiz.q: Who drafted the ESRS, and who adopted them?
options: Drafted by ESMA, adopted by Parliament
Drafted by EFRAG, adopted by the Commission as a delegated act
Drafted by the Commission, adopted by the Member States
Drafted by the ISSB, adopted by EFRAG
quiz.why: EFRAG provides technical advice; the Commission adopts the standards as a delegated regulation.
The materiality assessment identifies impacts on people and the environment and the risks and opportunities for the company.

quiz.q: For which financial year do the revised ESRS replace Set 1 for all reporters?
quiz.why: The revised standards are mandatory from financial year 2027. For 2026, companies may choose between Set 1 and early use of the revised set.
